materials.faqs:
Q: When do I need A350 LF2 instead of A105?
A: A350 LF2 is required whenever your minimum design metal temperature drops below roughly -29°C (-20°F), because it carries mandatory Charpy V-notch impact testing to verify the steel won't fail brittlely at that temperature - A105 has no such requirement and is not qualified for cold service.

Q: What's the maximum service temperature for A105?
A: Approximately 427°C (800°F) per ASME B16.5's material group tables; beyond that, strength drops enough that a Cr-Mo alloy grade (F11/F22) is typically specified instead.

Q: Is A105 the same as A105N?
A: "A105N" reflects normalized heat treatment, which most mills now apply as standard practice; functionally for most piping specifications, current A105 supply is normalized. Confirm heat treatment condition on your MTC.

materials.faqs:
Q: When is 304 sufficient and when do I actually need 316?
A: 304 handles most general chemical, food, and atmospheric service well. Move to 316 specifically when chlorides are present - coastal/marine atmospheres, saline process fluids, or chloride-containing cleaning agents - since 316's molybdenum addition meaningfully improves pitting resistance in exactly that condition.

Q: Why choose 304L over standard 304 for a welded assembly?
A: 304L's lower carbon ceiling (0.030% max vs 0.08% max) reduces the risk of chromium carbide precipitation at grain boundaries during welding (sensitization), which otherwise leaves the heat-affected zone vulnerable to intergranular corrosion.

materials.faqs:
Q: Does 316 fully resist seawater corrosion?
A: Not indefinitely in stagnant or crevice conditions - 316 resists general seawater corrosion well but can still pit or crevice-corrode in low-flow, oxygen-depleted pockets over long exposure. For continuous seawater immersion service, duplex or super duplex grades are typically specified instead.

Q: What's the practical difference between 316 and 316L in a bolted (non-welded) flange?
A: Very little, since sensitization risk is a welding phenomenon - for a flange that will be bolted rather than welded to the pipe (e.g., certain lap joint configurations), standard 316 is often adequate; 316L's real value shows up on flanges that will be butt-welded.

materials.faqs:
Q: Why do I need a stabilized grade instead of plain 304/316?
A: Above roughly 425-815°C, unstabilized austenitic grades are vulnerable to sensitization even without welding - simply holding at that temperature range lets chromium carbides precipitate at grain boundaries. Titanium (321) or niobium (347) ties up the carbon preferentially, protecting the chromium and preserving corrosion resistance in sustained high-temperature service.

Q: 321 or 347 - which should I specify?
A: 347 (niobium-stabilized) is generally preferred for refinery and heat-exchanger applications requiring resistance to knife-line attack near welds; 321 (titanium-stabilized) is more common in aerospace-adjacent and general high-temp piping. Both perform similarly for most industrial furnace piping - check your project spec for a named preference.

materials.faqs:
Q: Is Duplex 2205 the same as S31803 or S32205?
A: Both UNS numbers are sold commercially as "2205" and both fall under ASTM A182 Grade F51, but they're not identical: S32205 is the tighter, modern re-registration of the chemistry, with a higher nitrogen minimum (0.14% vs 0.08%) and narrower chromium/molybdenum ranges than the original S31803. Check your MTC for the specific UNS designation your project requires.

Q: Can duplex 2205 flanges be used above 315°C continuously?
A: Not recommended for sustained service - duplex stainless steels are susceptible to sigma-phase embrittlement in the 300-1000°C range with long exposure, which degrades toughness. Most specifications cap continuous duplex service around 300-315°C; consult your engineering specification for the exact limit on your project.

Q: Why is PMI testing particularly important for duplex flanges?
A: Duplex and 316 stainless can look visually similar and duplex costs meaningfully more, so mix-ups do happen in stock yards and during fabrication. Positive material identification (XRF or OES) at receiving and before installation is standard practice to confirm you actually received duplex, not 316.

materials.faqs:
Q: What is PREN and why does it matter for super duplex?
A: PREN (Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number) estimates a stainless steel's resistance to localized pitting corrosion, calculated as %Cr + 3.3x%Mo + 16x%N. Super duplex grades like F53 target a PREN above 40, meaningfully higher than standard 2205's ~35, which is why F53 is specified for more aggressive chloride environments like seawater cooling and desalination.

Q: Is super duplex 2507 always necessary, or is standard 2205 enough?
A: Standard 2205 (F51) handles most chemical processing and moderate marine exposure well. Reach for super duplex specifically when the environment is more aggressive - continuous seawater immersion, high-chloride produced water, or desalination brine - where the extra PREN margin genuinely changes service life.

materials.faqs:
Q: Why does F91 need a specific normalize-and-temper heat treatment?
A: F91's fine martensitic microstructure - the source of its high-temperature creep strength - only develops correctly through controlled normalizing followed by tempering. Skipping or mis-executing this heat treatment produces a flange that looks correct dimensionally and chemically but does not have the specified creep-rupture properties. Always request the heat treatment record on your MTC.

Q: Is F91 interchangeable with F22 at high temperature?
A: No - F91 is specified precisely because it out-performs F11/F22 at temperatures above roughly 550°C where those Cr-Mo grades' creep strength falls off. Substituting F22 for a design calling for F91 would under-rate the joint; confirm material grade against your P-T design basis, not just "alloy steel" generically.

standards.faqs:
Q: What size range does ASME B16.5 cover?
A: NPS 1/2 inch through NPS 24 inch, across seven pressure classes: 150, 300, 400, 600, 900, 1500, and 2500. Larger diameters, NPS 26 and above, fall under the companion standard ASME B16.47 instead.

Q: Do all six flange types share the same outside diameter and bolt circle?
A: Yes, for a given NPS and class, slip-on, weld neck, blind, socket weld, threaded, and lap joint flanges all share identical outside diameter, bolt circle diameter, and bolt hole pattern, so they bolt up to any matching flange regardless of type. What differs between types is the hub and bore geometry, not the bolting.

Q: What's the difference between Class 400 and Class 300 in practice?
A: Class 400 sits between 300 and 600 but is rarely specified for new construction - it exists largely for compatibility with legacy ASME B16.1 cast iron flanges. Most new projects choose 300 or step directly to 600 rather than specifying 400.

Q: What's the critical difference between Series A and Series B flanges?
A: They are dimensionally different standards for the same nominal sizes - Series A (based on MSS SP-44) generally has a larger outside diameter and different bolting than Series B (based on API 605) at the same NPS and class. A Series A flange will NOT bolt up correctly to a Series B flange of the same nominal size - this mismatch is a documented, real field error, so the series must be specified explicitly on every purchase order, never assumed.

Q: Which series is more common - A or B?
A: It varies by industry and region rather than following a universal rule; refining and large-diameter transmission piping projects frequently specify one or the other by company standard. Always confirm the required series from your project's piping specification rather than defaulting.

standards.faqs:
Q: Is PN16 the same pressure rating as ASME Class 150?
A: They're commonly treated as roughly equivalent for general reference, but PN and Class ratings are each their own dimensional and pressure-temperature system - the actual allowable pressure at a given temperature depends on material group under each standard separately. Use a proper cross-reference for the specific material and temperature, not a straight PN-to-Class substitution, when the application is pressure-critical.

Q: Can I bolt an EN 1092-1 flange to an ASME B16.5 flange?
A: Not directly in most cases - bolt circle diameter, number of bolts, and bolt hole diameter differ between the two standards even at nominally "equivalent" ratings. A reducing or transition spool is typically required to mate EN and ASME flanges; don't assume compatibility without checking both dimension tables.

industries.faqs:
Q: What does NACE MR0175 sour-service compliance actually require?
A: It sets hardness limits on both the flange material and the bolting to resist sulfide stress cracking in H2S-containing service - for bolting specifically, this typically means B7M (a softer, controlled-hardness version of standard B7) rather than standard B7 studs. Confirm your project's specific NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 compliance requirements at order time.

Q: Which flange materials suit sour (H2S) service?
A: Carbon steel A105 and Cr-Mo alloys can be qualified for sour service with the correct heat treatment and hardness control; for more aggressive sour/high-chloride combined environments, duplex or super duplex grades are frequently specified instead.

industries.faqs:
Q: How do I choose between 316L, duplex, and a nickel alloy for a chemical line?
A: As a general progression: 316L covers most general chemical service; move to duplex or super duplex when chlorides or higher mechanical strength are the driver; reserve nickel alloys (Inconel, Hastelloy, Monel) for specific aggressive media - strong acids, HF, or combined high-temperature corrosion - where stainless and duplex are documented to fall short. Share your process fluid, concentration, and temperature for a specific material recommendation.
